name: NLRC4-associated autoinflammation with macrophage activation syndrome

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by gain-of-function mutations in NLRC4, which encodes an inflammasome sensor, leading to constitutive inflammasome activation
Presents in infancy with recurrent fevers, severe secretory enterocolitis, and a strong predisposition to macrophage activation syndrome
Life-threatening macrophage activation syndrome (haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) can arise spontaneously or with intercurrent illness
Very high levels of interleukin-18 in blood are a distinctive biomarker that helps distinguish this from other inflammasomopathies
Enterocolitis may cause profuse diarrhoea, feeding intolerance, and failure to thrive in early infancy
Both interleukin-1 blockade and interleukin-18 directed strategies are used, and IL-1 blockade is a cornerstone of therapy
Prompt recognition and treatment of macrophage activation syndrome is essential given its high mortality
reference.pathophysiology: This disease is driven by gain-of-function mutations in NLRC4, a cytosolic pattern-recognition receptor that forms an inflammasome. The mutant sensor triggers constitutive inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation, producing excess interleukin-1 beta and, characteristically, very large amounts of interleukin-18. Pyroptotic cell death and cytokine release cause severe intestinal inflammation (infantile enterocolitis) and a strong tendency toward macrophage activation syndrome. The dominant role of interleukin-1 and interleukin-18 explains the use of IL-1 blockade and IL-18 targeted approaches.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis with macrophage activation syndrome
Other inflammasomopathies such as familial Mediterranean fever
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for NLRC4 gain-of-function mutations
Serum interleukin-18 level, characteristically markedly elevated
Ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, and blood counts to detect macrophage activation syndrome
Endoscopy and intestinal biopsy for enterocolitis
Bone marrow examination for haemophagocytosis when indicated
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome: rising ferritin, falling cell counts, coagulopathy
Severe enterocolitis with dehydration and failure to thrive
Rapid deterioration during an intercurrent infection
reference.prognosis: The disease carries significant mortality risk, principally from macrophage activation syndrome, but early recognition with interleukin-1 blockade and interleukin-18 directed therapy has improved outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing evolving macrophage activation syndrome by not tracking ferritin and blood counts
Attributing severe infantile diarrhoea solely to inflammatory bowel disease or infection
Overlooking the diagnostic value of a markedly raised interleukin-18 level
Delaying interleukin-1 blockade during a hyperinflammatory crisis
management: Establish interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra as the cornerstone of therapy for the constitutive inflammasome activation
Add interleukin-18-directed treatment with recombinant interleukin-18 binding protein (tadekinig alfa) given the hallmark very high interleukin-18
Treat life-threatening macrophage activation syndrome with corticosteroids and interferon-gamma neutralisation (emapalumab) supported by critical care
Support the infantile enterocolitis with fluid and electrolyte resuscitation and parenteral nutrition during profuse secretory diarrhoea and feeding intolerance
Monitor for macrophage activation with serial ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen and blood counts, escalating promptly on deterioration
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across clinical immunology, rheumatology and intensive care
Provide genetic counselling for the gain-of-function NLRC4 variant
